extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent applicants/attorneys (prosecution practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating enablement and utility under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) and 35 U.S.C. 101 in utility patent applications, with particular attention to computer-programming disclosures, affidavits, prior art citations, and claim scope. Intended to direct examiners on burdens of proof, appropriate rejections, and acceptable applicant rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach how to practice claimed method
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be adequate to teach how to practice the claimed method. If such practice requires a particular apparatus, then the application must provide a sufficient disclosure of that apparatus if such is not already available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing method claims (including computer-implemented methods), examiners should ensure the specification enables practice of the method without undue experimentation; disclosure of required apparatus is necessary if not already known in the art. (Cited: In re Ghiron; In re Gunn.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Record support for nonenabling findings and reasonable challenge to applicant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When USPTO personnel question the adequacy of computer system or computer programming disclosures, the reasons for finding the specification to be nonenabling should be supported by the record as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must present a reasonable basis or evidence for challenging disclosures and must reasonably challenge applicant-submitted evidence (e.g., affidavits). If an affidavit is unchallenged and no record basis exists, a 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection may not be sustained. (Cited: In re Naquin; In re Morehouse.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge disclosures that omit programmed steps/algorithms/procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An examining guideline is to challenge the sufficiency of disclosures that fail to include the programmed steps, algorithms or procedures that the computer performs necessary to produce the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmed steps can be described in any understandable way (e.g., reasonably detailed flowcharts). As complexity and generality of components increase, the basis for challenging a bare flowchart strengthens because more than routine experimentation may be required to implement a working program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant burden to show enablement after reasonable basis advanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis or presented evidence to question the adequacy of a disclosure, the applicant must show that the specification would enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical applicant responses include submitting affidavits, referencing prior art patents or technical publications, presenting arguments of counsel, or combinations of these approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits must be critically analyzed for relevance and factual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: In computer cases, affidavits must be critically analyzed; examine the skill level and/or qualifications of the affiant relative to the person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an affiant's skill level differs from the PHOSITA, the affidavit may be insufficient unless it demonstrates the amount of experimentation required by a PHOSITA to implement the invention. Affiants that are over- or under-qualified may misstate the experimentation required; the affidavit must be probative of PHOSITA skill as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits must provide factual support, not mere conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits that merely state conclusions or opinions about enablement without supporting facts are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits should include factual evidence (e.g., number of programmers needed, man-hours, level of skill, details of steps taken) rather than conclusory statements that components are "well-known" or "could be constructed." Opinion evidence on the ultimate legal question of enablement is not sufficient to rebut a prima facie case of nonenablement. (Cited: In re Brandstadter; Hirschfield; In re Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits must reflect knowledge as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: For an affidavit to be relevant to enablement, it must be probative of the level of skill of the person of ordinary skill in the art as of the time the applicant filed his application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits stating what was known at the time the affidavit was executed rather than at filing are insufficient. (Cited: In re Gunn.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial availability and clarity of prior art use for enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is pertinent to enablement, but merely citing publications may not be sufficient to meet the applicant’s burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing excerpts from technical publications is insufficient unless it is clear which parts of the cited material could be used and how they would be interconnected to construct the claimed device. This is less critical when the cited components are standard parts of an identified prior-art system and a standard device attached thereto. (Cited: In re Forman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art patents/publications must predate the application's effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art patents and patent application publications relied on to show the state of the art for enablement must have a publication date earlier than the effective filing date of the application under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents issued after the filing date are not evidence of subject matter known to PHOSITA at the filing date because their subject matter may have been known only to patentees and the PTO. (Cited: In re Budnick; In re Gunn.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of prior-art components required to show enablement by old components
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely showing that components enumerated in a block diagram were old does not demonstrate how each would be interconnected to function in a complex combination; the specification must set forth the integration of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not set forth how prior-art components interconnect to produce the claimed results, undue experimentation may be required. Patents used to show components are "old" must be analyzed for germane relevance and whether they provide better detail than the applicant’s disclosure. Also, known programming techniques do not establish enablement unless they are of similar complexity to the disclosed techniques. (Cited: In re Scarbrough; In re Knowlton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments of counsel cannot substitute for evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel may be effective in establishing examiner error, but arguments alone cannot take the place of evidence in the record once an examiner has advanced a reasonable basis for questioning the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record consists substantially of attorney opinions, the court has indicated that factual affidavits could provide important evidence; arguments of counsel should be supplemented with factual evidence where enablement is contested. (Cited: In re Budnick; In re Schulze; In re Cole; In re Knowlton; In re Wiseman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101) differs from enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101; 101 requires some specific, substantial, and credible use, while 112(a) requires an indication of how that use can be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections under 112(a) based on grounds other than "lack of utility" should be imposed separately from any rejection due to "lack of utility" under 35 U.S.C. 101. If an invention lacks utility (101), it also fails the how-to-use aspect of enablement (112(a)). See MPEP § 2107 for more on utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden to provide reasonable basis for nonutility/nonenablement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner concludes that an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility; only after the examiner provides evidence showing a PHOSITA would reasonably doubt the asserted utility does the burden shift to the applicant to rebut. (Cited: In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana; In re Bundy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal standard for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 has been properly imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence required; the character and amount of evidence needed vary depending on the claim and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established scientific principles. The applicant's evidence need only make it more likely than not that the asserted utility is true—not "beyond a reasonable doubt." (Cited: In re Oetiker; In re Gazave; In re Chilowsky; In re Irons; MPEP § 2107.02.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility satisfied but enablement still required
rubrics_metrics.description: In some instances, the utility of the claimed invention will be provided, but the skilled artisan will not know how to effect that use; in such a case no rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 101, but a rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention may be highly useful yet not enabled if the specification fails to teach one skilled in the art how to use it. (Cited: Mowry v. Whitney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims (use Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter. USPTO personnel will use the Wands factors to ascertain whether the amount of experimentation required to enable the full scope of the claimed invention is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first step is to determine exactly what subject matter is encompassed by the claims (considering claim as a whole, and dependent claims per 35 U.S.C. 112(d)). The focus is whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled. See Guidelines for Assessing Enablement (Jan 10, 2024) and MPEP §§ 2164.01(a), 2164.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach how to make/use full scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation' or that any experimentation must be 'reasonable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not everything necessary need be disclosed—what is well-known may be omitted. The scope of enablement must bear a 'reasonable correlation' to the scope of the claims. The more one claims, the more one must enable. (Cited: Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Wright; In re Buchner; In re Fisher.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Range and genus claims require reasonable enablement across claimed scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range; for genus claims, although not every variant must be described, the scope claimed must be reasonably enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification indicates certain values won't work or warns against portions of a range, yet claims encompass them, enablement may fail (e.g., AK Steel). Genus claims that claim overly broad embodiments when only a few examples are taught may be inadequately enabled (e.g., Amgen). Conversely, some claims (e.g., DNA encoding a specifically identified protein sequence) may be enabled if a skilled artisan could readily determine embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-of-enablement rejection must identify non-enabled claim subject matter and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: A scope-of-enablement rejection must identify the claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why the specification is not enabling, applying the Wands factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's explanation should include any unresolved questions the examiner posed that raise doubt as to enablement and show why those questions were not satisfactorily resolved. This is an enablement (112(a)) rejection, not a definiteness (112(b)) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of disclosure not dispositive: examples or broad terminology acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: An enabling disclosure may be set forth by specific example or broad terminology; the exact form of disclosure is not dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are not rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure for noninclusion of limitations that are presumed to be within ordinary skill; one does not look to the claims but to the specification to find out how to practice the claimed invention. (Cited: In re Marzocchi; In re Skrivan.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims interpreted in light of the specification; broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with spec
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing enabled scope, teachings of the specification must not be ignored; claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting claims in view of the specification does not mean everything in the specification must be read into the claims. The record must be clear so the public has notice of the patentee's scope of protection when the patent issues. (Cited: Raytheon Co. v. Roper; W.L. Gore & Assoc.; In re Johnson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case examples (Amgen/EPO analogs) as guidance for genus claim adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad claim scope (e.g., claiming all analogs or broad classes) requires commensurate enabling disclosure; disclosing only a few exemplars may not enable claiming all possible variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amgen illustrates that extensive but generic statements about many analogs are not sufficient if details for preparing only a few analogs are disclosed. The applicant must provide enabling disclosure commensurate with claim breadth, otherwise claims may be rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure.
